mcqs.question: A protocol uses bit stuffing with `01111110` as its frame delimiter. Why does it insert an extra 0 after any run of five consecutive 1s in the actual data?
options: To synchronize the sender and receiver's clocks
To compress the data before transmission
To add a parity check to every six bits of data
To guarantee the delimiter's exact bit pattern can never occur by accident inside the data itself, so the receiver can unambiguously find frame boundaries
mcqs.explanation: The extra 0 exists purely to prevent the data from ever accidentally containing the six-1s-in-a-row delimiter pattern, preserving unambiguous frame boundaries. It has nothing to do with compression, parity, or clock sync — those are separate concerns solved by other mechanisms.

mcqs.question: A receiver computes the CRC division on a received frame and gets a remainder of zero. What can it conclude?
options: No error pattern that this particular CRC is designed to detect was found — not an absolute guarantee of correctness
The frame definitely traveled over an error-free physical medium
The frame is guaranteed to be byte-for-byte identical to what was sent
The sender's generator polynomial must be different from the receiver's
mcqs.explanation: A zero remainder only means none of the error patterns the CRC is designed to catch were detected — it's a strong but not absolute guarantee, since some rare bit-flip combinations can coincidentally produce the same remainder. It says nothing about the medium being error-free, and a matching remainder actually implies both sides used the same generator polynomial.

mcqs.question: A one-way satellite broadcast (no return channel) needs error resilience. Why is forward error correction the right choice here instead of retransmission (ARQ)?
options: FEC is cheaper per bit sent than any retransmission scheme
There's no return channel to request a retransmission over, so error correction has to happen using only the redundant data already sent — ARQ is simply not possible
Satellite links never experience actual bit errors, so FEC is used only as a formality
ARQ requires a wired connection and cannot function over radio links
mcqs.explanation: The defining constraint is the missing return channel: ARQ fundamentally requires the ability to ask for a retransmit, which a one-way broadcast can't do, making FEC's self-contained correction the only option. FEC isn't cheaper per bit (it adds constant redundancy), satellite links do experience real errors, and ARQ works fine over radio when a return path exists.
